To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
hematuria and/or proteinuria are common findings in children, and the most common cause of hematuria is glomerular disease, while proteinuria is more often due to tubular disease.
the most common causes of gross hematuria and microscopic hematuria are primary glomerulonephritis and urinary tract infection.

the diagnosis in 90 percent of the cases of hematuria and/or proteinuria in children was made by the clinical history, physical examination, and urinalysis; the most frequent diagnosis was IgA nephropathy, which accounted for 50 percent of the cases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of new techniques in the field of renal pathology and the application of these new methods to the study of renal biopsy specimens.
the study of the renal disease and the diagnostic evaluation in children.
the diagnostic approach of hematuria and/or proteinuria in pediatric patients, with emphasis on the role of kidney biopsy in the diagnosis and management of renal disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in a child presenting with hematuria, proteinuria or both, the first step should be the exclusion of urinary tract infection.
the diagnosis of hematuria and/or proteinuria in children is a complex problem.
a child with proteinuria and hematuria, or either one, should be evaluated by a nephrologist and, if necessary, by a renal biopsy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the majority of children, the cause of hematuria and/or proteinuria can be determined by the use of non-invasive diagnostic tests.

in children with hematuria or proteinuria, the most important initial diagnostic step is to exclude urinary tract infection, and to determine the presence of hemoglobinuria, which is a very important clue to the diagnosis.

the diagnostic approach to pediatric patients with hematuria and/or proteinuria should be individualized, and the final diagnosis should be based on clinical and laboratory data, as well as on kidney biopsy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hematuria and/or proteinuria should be evaluated with a renal ultrasound and, if indicated, a renal biopsy.
a careful history, physical examination, and laboratory workup are necessary to identify patients with renal disease and to direct the proper evaluation.
the evaluation of a child with hematuria and/or proteinuria requires a systematic approach, and the diagnosis of a renal disease is not always easy.
